steps.text: # zig as this app's C toolchain, so an unattended install needs no root
# and no system compiler (design.md 11.0 item 15). The name it is called
# by picks the mode. Two things have to be corrected on the way:
#  - a Rust target triple (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu), which cc-rs passes
#    as --target= and zig's parser rejects, becomes zig's;
#  - the glibc version is pinned to this machine's, or zig links against
#    the newest glibc it knows and the program will not start here
case ${0##*/} in *++) m=c++ ;; ar) m=ar ;; *) m=cc ;; esac
if [ -n "$t" ]; then a=--target=$t; else a=--target=$(printf %s "${a#--target=}" | sed 's/-unknown-/-/'); fi

steps.run: cd "{runtime_dir}/ibcc" && chmod 755 cc && for t in gcc clang c++ g++ clang++ ar; do cp cc "$t"; done

recipes.min_os: Linux amd64, kernel 3.2+, glibc 2.17+ (highest GLIBC symbol version checked: 2.17)
recipes.notes: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu. Layout: the tarball is rust-installer format 3 (rust-installer-version = 3 in all 16 planned files): rust-<ver>-<triple>/{components,install.sh,manifest.in per component,...} with each component in rust-<ver>-<triple>/<component>/{bin,lib,libexec,etc,share}. install.sh only copies <component>/<path> to <prefix>/<path> for each file:/dir: line of manifest.in (bin 755, others 644), writes bookkeeping into lib/rustlib/ (components, manifest-*, install.log, uninstall.sh, rust-installer-version, none needed at run time) and on Linux runs ldconfig. The components never overlap (checked: 0 duplicate paths across components, no symlinks in the Linux, Windows or macOS tarballs), so unpacking with strip_components 2 merges every component straight into {runtime_dir}: entries with only 1-2 path parts (top-level install.sh, components, etc.) are dropped; each component's manifest.in lands on {runtime_dir}/manifest.in and overwrites the previous one (harmless, delete it if tidy). The unpacker must skip entries with fewer path parts than strip_components and keep Unix modes. TESTED on Linux amd64: the file tree and modes from this unpack are identical to install.sh's apart from the bookkeeping files. Run the toolchain with an explicit environment in the app's own process only (never PATH/registry/profile changes): CARGO_HOME={runtime_dir}/cargo-home (or an app-owned writable dir; cargo writes its registry index, crate cache and installed binaries there, default is ~/.cargo), RUSTC={runtime_dir}/bin/rustc and RUSTDOC={runtime_dir}/bin/rustdoc (TESTED: without RUSTC or {runtime_dir}/bin on PATH, cargo fails with 'could not execute process `rustc -vV`' - it does NOT look next to itself, and with a user's rustup on PATH it would silently use the user's rustc), and prepend {runtime_dir}/bin to PATH in that process so `cargo clippy`/`cargo fmt` find cargo-clippy/cargo-fmt (tested). RUSTUP_HOME is not used at all: this is a plain toolchain with no rustup proxies; set it to {runtime_dir}/rustup-home and unset RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN only as belt-and-braces. Clear inherited RUSTFLAGS, RUSTDOCFLAGS, CARGO_BUILD_*, CARGO_TARGET_DIR, CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS and RUSTC_WRAPPER, which a user's global environment would inject. Cargo also reads .cargo/config.toml from the project dir and EVERY parent directory (then $CARGO_HOME/config.toml), so a project under a user's home picks up ~/.cargo/config.toml; keep app projects outside home or accept that. rustc finds its sysroot from its own location (tested: `rustc --print sysroot` = the folder it was run from) and binaries use RUNPATH $ORIGIN/../lib on Linux, so no LD_LIBRARY_PATH is needed. Slim alternative (tested on Linux, 601 MB and 156 files instead of ~1.9 GB and ~66,000 files; rust-docs alone is 727 MB / 67,212 HTML files and is only present in some tarballs): unpack with strip_components 1 into {tmp}, then copy only rustc, rust-std-<triple>, cargo and optionally clippy-preview and rustfmt-preview, e.g. `cp -R "{tmp}/rustc/." "{runtime_dir}/"` per component on POSIX or `xcopy "{tmp}\rustc" "{runtime_dir}\" /E /I /Y /Q` per component in cmd. rust-analyzer-preview, llvm-tools-preview, rust-analysis, rust-docs-json-preview and llvm-bitcode-linker-preview are not needed to build. TESTED (Linux amd64, Ubuntu 24.04, normal user): direct unpack to '<scratch>/a b/copy1', a second identical copy side by side in '<scratch>/a b/copy2', a slim copy, and an install.sh result moved to '<scratch>/a b/sh-moved': in every one `cargo new`, `cargo run` (Hello, world!), `cargo test`, `cargo build` with a crates.io dependency (itoa), `cargo clippy`, `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo doc` succeeded with HOME and TMPDIR pointed at empty sentinel folders, which stayed empty; all caches landed in the per-copy CARGO_HOME. install.sh alternative (also tested): `sh install.sh --prefix=<dir> --disable-ldconfig` works but CANNOT take a prefix containing a space (it word-splits its own arguments: `--prefix=/a b/x` fails with "Option 'b/x' is not recognized", quoting does not help), and without --disable-ldconfig it runs ldconfig as root, rebuilding the system /etc/ld.so.cache (and, only for prefix /usr/local, writes /etc/ld.so.conf.d/rust-installer-v1-rustlib.conf). An install.sh result moved afterwards into a path with a space still works (tested); only the uninstall bookkeeping holds absolute paths. The direct unpack avoids all of this. Added 2026-09-20 (design.md 11.0 item 15): on Linux the C toolchain is zig, a companion runtime (policy `requires`), not the system compiler, so an unattended install needs no root and works on a machine with no gcc at all. The steps write a small POSIX shim into {runtime_dir}/ibcc under every name a build might call (cc, gcc, clang, c++, g++, clang++, ar); it execs `zig cc`/`zig c++`/`zig ar` and rewrites a Rust target triple (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) to zig's (x86_64-linux-gnu), which cc-rs passes as --target= and zig's parser rejects. {runtime_dir}/ibcc goes first on PATH for the project install only. Tested on this machine with only the shim on PATH: cargo built a crate with a cc-rs build step and ran it, and nim compiled and linked a program using std/httpclient. Added 2026-09-20 (design.md 11.0 item 15): on Linux the C toolchain is zig, a companion runtime (policy `requires`), not the system compiler, so an unattended install needs no root and works on a machine with no gcc at all. The steps write a small POSIX shim into {runtime_dir}/ibcc under every name a build might call (cc, gcc, clang, c++, g++, clang++, ar); it execs `zig cc`/`zig c++`/`zig ar` and rewrites a Rust target triple (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) to zig's (x86_64-linux-gnu), which cc-rs passes as --target= and zig's parser rejects, and pins the target glibc to this machine's (getconf GNU_LIBC_VERSION), without which zig links against the newest glibc it knows and the program will not start on an older system (measured on CentOS 7: "version GLIBC_2.18 not found"). {runtime_dir}/ibcc goes first on PATH for the project install only. Tested on this machine with only the shim on PATH: cargo built a crate with a cc-rs build step and ran it, and nim compiled and linked a program using std/httpclient.

recipes.min_os: Windows 10+ / Server 2016+ (platform-support page; i686 needs a Pentium 4/SSE2). Checked in 1.98.1 x86_64: rustc_driver and std DLLs import WaitOnAddress/WakeByAddress* (api-ms-win-core-synch-l1-2-0.dll), GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime and ProcessPrng (bcryptprimitives.dll), so they cannot load on Windows 7; PE headers say 5.2, which is not the real floor. Programs it builds need Windows 10 too (same imports, checked on cross-built x86_64 and i686 executables). The bundled ld.exe, dlltool.exe and gcc.exe (MinGW-Builds GCC 14.2.0, binutils 2.44) import GetFinalPathNameByHandleA, i.e. Vista+.
recipes.notes: x86_64-pc-windows-gnu. Same rust-installer format-3 layout as the -msvc file, so the same strip_components 2 unpack applies (checked: 1.98.1 x86_64 tarball, 303 MB, 2.7 GB unpacked with docs). Components: cargo, clippy-preview, llvm-bitcode-linker-preview, llvm-tools-preview, rust-analysis, rust-analyzer-preview, rustc, rust-docs, rust-docs-json-preview, rustfmt-preview, rust-mingw, rust-std. rust-mingw puts a link-only x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc.exe/i686-w64-mingw32-gcc.exe, ld.exe, dlltool.exe and libwinpthread-1.dll in lib\rustlib\x86_64-pc-windows-gnu\bin\self-contained, and crt2.o, dllcrt2.o, libgcc*.a, libmingw32/mingwex/msvcrt.a and 40 Windows import libraries (kernel32, advapi32, bcrypt, ws2_32, userenv, ntdll, synchronization, user32, gdi32, ole32, oleaut32, shell32, crypt32, winhttp, iphlpapi, secur32, ...) in lib\rustlib\x86_64-pc-windows-gnu\lib\self-contained. The C runtime is msvcrt.dll, not UCRT. TESTED (cross-built from Linux with the same std and rust-mingw files, linked by rust-lld in self-contained mode, since this host can't run the Windows ld.exe): hello world with threads for x86_64 and i686; a cargo project using serde, serde_json, regex, rand 0.8, clap 4, anyhow, windows-sys 0.59 and 0.61 (windows-link raw-dylib) and windows 0.58 built for both, once a dlltool was provided; without one it failed with "error calling dlltool". On Windows the dlltool.exe in self-contained must be on PATH (project_install.path_prepend does this). What breaks: (1) crates that compile C/C++ through the cc crate (ring, rustls' default aws-lc-rs, libsqlite3-sys bundled, zstd-sys, openssl-src...): the bundled gcc.exe is link-only (its own GCC-WARNING.txt says so), so they need a full MinGW-w64 GCC, e.g. the catalogue's WinLibs gcc (tested from Linux: ring + a cc build script built and linked against WinLibs 16.2.0 UCRT headers and libraries; Rust std also linked against WinLibs 10.5.0 MSVCRT libraries); (2) crates or build scripts that link a Windows library outside the 40 bundled import libraries (e.g. d3d11, dxgi, dwmapi, version, shlwapi, ncrypt) with #[link] or cargo:rustc-link-lib: most crates now use windows-sys/windows-link raw-dylib or the winapi/windows-targets crates, which carry their own import libraries, so this is rare; WinLibs has them all; (3) crates that only support MSVC (anything linking prebuilt .lib files, e.g. some vendor SDK bindings). Run the toolchain with an explicit environment in the app's own process only, as for the -msvc recipe: CARGO_HOME in an app-owned folder, RUSTC/RUSTDOC pointing into {runtime_dir}\bin, {runtime_dir}\bin first on PATH, and inherited RUSTFLAGS, RUSTDOCFLAGS, CARGO_BUILD_*, CARGO_TARGET_DIR, CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS and RUSTC_WRAPPER cleared. Cargo still reads .cargo/config.toml from the project folder and every parent. Slim copy: rust-docs, rust-docs-json-preview, rust-analysis, rust-analyzer-preview, llvm-tools-preview and llvm-bitcode-linker-preview are not needed to build; keep rust-mingw.

project_install.notes: Builds the app on the user's machine at install time (installer-builder design.md 1.8). Without RUSTC cargo can't find rustc (tested). Links with the toolchain's own rust-mingw linker and import libraries, so pure-Rust crates need nothing else. The self-contained folder is put on PATH so rustc finds dlltool.exe, which raw-dylib crates (windows-link, windows-sys 0.60+) need on -gnu: as far as rustc's source shows (find_binutils_dlltool) it looks for dlltool.exe on PATH, not in its sysroot; not tested on Windows. Without a dlltool a Linux cross-build failed with 'error calling dlltool'. rustc ignores linkers under its own sysroot when deciding self-contained linking, so this PATH entry doesn't change that. Crates that compile C/C++ (ring, bundled SQLite, zstd-sys...) need a real MinGW-w64 GCC: prepend the catalogue's WinLibs mingw64\bin as well; rustc then links with it instead of the bundled files.

Programs it builds need Windows 10 too (same imports, checked on cross-built x86_64 and i686 executables). The bundled ld.exe, dlltool.exe and gcc.exe (MinGW-Builds GCC 14.2.0, binutils 2.44) import GetFinalPathNameByHandleA, i.e. Vista+.
recipes.notes: i686-pc-windows-gnu. Same rust-installer format-3 layout as the -msvc file, so the same strip_components 2 unpack applies (checked: 1.98.1 x86_64 tarball, 303 MB, 2.7 GB unpacked with docs). Components: cargo, clippy-preview, llvm-bitcode-linker-preview, llvm-tools-preview, rust-analysis, rust-analyzer-preview, rustc, rust-docs, rust-docs-json-preview, rustfmt-preview, rust-mingw, rust-std. rust-mingw puts a link-only x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc.exe/i686-w64-mingw32-gcc.exe, ld.exe, dlltool.exe and libwinpthread-1.dll in lib\rustlib\i686-pc-windows-gnu\bin\self-contained, and crt2.o, dllcrt2.o, libgcc*.a, libmingw32/mingwex/msvcrt.a and 40 Windows import libraries (kernel32, advapi32, bcrypt, ws2_32, userenv, ntdll, synchronization, user32, gdi32, ole32, oleaut32, shell32, crypt32, winhttp, iphlpapi, secur32, ...) in lib\rustlib\i686-pc-windows-gnu\lib\self-contained. The C runtime is msvcrt.dll, not UCRT. TESTED (cross-built from Linux with the same std and rust-mingw files, linked by rust-lld in self-contained mode, since this host can't run the Windows ld.exe): hello world with threads for x86_64 and i686; a cargo project using serde, serde_json, regex, rand 0.8, clap 4, anyhow, windows-sys 0.59 and 0.61 (windows-link raw-dylib) and windows 0.58 built for both, once a dlltool was provided; without one it failed with "error calling dlltool". On Windows the dlltool.exe in self-contained must be on PATH (project_install.path_prepend does this). What breaks: (1) crates that compile C/C++ through the cc crate (ring, rustls' default aws-lc-rs, libsqlite3-sys bundled, zstd-sys, openssl-src...): the bundled gcc.exe is link-only (its own GCC-WARNING.txt says so), so they need a full MinGW-w64 GCC, e.g. the catalogue's WinLibs gcc (tested from Linux: ring + a cc build script built and linked against WinLibs 16.2.0 UCRT headers and libraries; Rust std also linked against WinLibs 10.5.0 MSVCRT libraries); (2) crates or build scripts that link a Windows library outside the 40 bundled import libraries (e.g. d3d11, dxgi, dwmapi, version, shlwapi, ncrypt) with #[link] or cargo:rustc-link-lib: most crates now use windows-sys/windows-link raw-dylib or the winapi/windows-targets crates, which carry their own import libraries, so this is rare; WinLibs has them all; (3) crates that only support MSVC (anything linking prebuilt .lib files, e.g. some vendor SDK bindings). Run the toolchain with an explicit environment in the app's own process only, as for the -msvc recipe: CARGO_HOME in an app-owned folder, RUSTC/RUSTDOC pointing into {runtime_dir}\bin, {runtime_dir}\bin first on PATH, and inherited RUSTFLAGS, RUSTDOCFLAGS, CARGO_BUILD_*, CARGO_TARGET_DIR, CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS and RUSTC_WRAPPER cleared. Cargo still reads .cargo/config.toml from the project folder and every parent. Slim copy: rust-docs, rust-docs-json-preview, rust-analysis, rust-analyzer-preview, llvm-tools-preview and llvm-bitcode-linker-preview are not needed to build; keep rust-mingw.

launch.notes: The app is the program built by project_install and runs directly.

project_install.notes: Builds the app on the user's machine at install time (installer-builder design.md 1.8). Without RUSTC cargo can't find rustc (tested). Links with the toolchain's own rust-mingw linker and import libraries, so pure-Rust crates need nothing else. The self-contained folder is put on PATH so rustc finds dlltool.exe, which raw-dylib crates (windows-link, windows-sys 0.60+) need on -gnu: as far as rustc's source shows (find_binutils_dlltool) it looks for dlltool.exe on PATH, not in its sysroot; not tested on Windows. Without a dlltool a Linux cross-build failed with 'error calling dlltool'. rustc ignores linkers under its own sysroot when deciding self-contained linking, so this PATH entry doesn't change that. Crates that compile C/C++ (ring, bundled SQLite, zstd-sys...) need a real MinGW-w64 GCC: prepend the catalogue's WinLibs mingw64\bin as well; rustc then links with it instead of the bundled files.
